# Ayogharajātaka (Ja 510)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ayogharajātaka* (Ja 510) is a narrative belonging to the *Vīsatinipāta* of the Jātaka collection (PTS Ja IV 491–499) [Morris 1882; Lang 2003; Fausböll 1887]. It exemplifies the Bodhisatta's perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*) [Warren 1896; Fausböll 1877; Hazra 1994]. According to the nidāna framing preserved in the commentary, the Buddha related this past birth when discussing his own Great Renunciation (*mahānekkhamma*), remarking that he had similarly abandoned a kingdom in previous lives [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as the son of King Brahmadatta of Benares [Fausböll 1897; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Because a female goblin (*yakkhī*) had devoured the queen's first two children, the king had an iron house (*ayoghara*) constructed where the queen gave birth and the child was raised, earning him the name Prince Ayoghara [Fausböll 1887; Hazra 1994; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Upon coming of age at sixteen, the prince is shown the city and offered the kingdom, but realizes that no worldly fortress can shield mortals from aging, disease, and death [Anandajoti 2010; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Refusing the throne, he delivers a discourse on the certainty of death and renounces the household life, leading his parents and many subjects to become ascetics with him [Lang 2003; Hazra 1994; War Yar Mein Da 2015].
The episode is closely adapted in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (III.3, *Ayoghara-cariya*) as a paramount model of *nekkhammapāramī* [Bareau, Les récits canoniques; Morris 1882; Hazra 1994]. Verses from the text share direct canonical parallels with the Gāndhārī Dharmapada (G3-Dhp 51–60, G-Dhp 139–161), the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (UV 1, *Anityavarga*), Chinese versions of the Dharmapada/Udāna (T 212, T 213), the *Theragāthā* (Thag 4.10), and the *Mahādhammapālajātaka* (Ja 447) [SuttaCentral; Barua 1921]. It is also cited in exegetical works such as the *Peṭakopadesa* and *Nettippakaraṇa* [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus shows extensive textual reuse across the Pali commentary tradition—most prominently with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, and grammatical treatises like the *Saddanīti*—alongside cross-language alignments with Āryaśūra's Sanskrit *Jātakamālā* and its Tibetan translation [DharmaNexus; Lang 2003].
